signIn.title: Sign in
signIn.intro: Use the same account as for the classic openmediavault interface.

signIn.lockedTitle: Check the password before trying again
signIn.lockedBody: After repeated failed sign-ins the server can lock an account. Waiting does not unlock it, and this page cannot either. Ask another administrator to unlock the account. If it is the only administrator account, someone with access to the server's own screen and keyboard has to reset it there.

signIn.rejectedBody: Check the user name and password, then try again.
signIn.unreachableBody: Check that the server is switched on and connected to the network, then try again.

totp.rejectedBody: Enter the code your authenticator app shows now. Each code works for only 30 seconds.

about.title: About this interface
about.body: This is an unofficial community plugin that adds a new web interface to openmediavault. It is not made by the openmediavault project, and it changes nothing about how openmediavault works or how secure it is.

checklist.title: Set up your NAS
checklist.intro: A few things to check after installing. Each item is read from the NAS's current settings.

password.title: Change the factory password
password.body: openmediavault is installed with a password that anyone can look up. If it has not been changed yet, change it now. This page cannot check whether it has been.
password.bodyOtherAdmin: openmediavault is installed with a password for the admin account that anyone can look up. This page cannot check whether it has been changed. To change it, sign in as admin and open Your account.

https.title: Use a secure connection (HTTPS)
https.doneOnHttp: HTTPS is on, but this page was opened without it.
https.secureNoLink: Open this page with an address that starts with https://.
https.notDone: HTTPS is off. The notice at the top of the page says why that matters. Turning it on needs a certificate, which the classic interface can create.
https.link: Open Web interface settings in the classic interface
https.readFailed: Could not read the web interface settings.

email.title: Get email alerts
email.off: Alerts are off. Turn them on to hear about failing disks, full file systems and available updates. You need the details of an email account the NAS can send from.
email.incomplete: Alerts are on, but some details are missing, so none can be sent.
email.applyHint: After saving there, apply the changes, then send a test email.
email.link: Open Notifications in the classic interface
email.readFailed: Could not read the email alert settings.

name.link: Change it in the classic interface

timezone.link: Change it in the classic interface

ssh.title: SSH
ssh.intro: SSH lets you sign in to the NAS from another computer and type commands. It is for advanced tasks; most people never need it.
ssh.pendingOnArrival: Saved SSH settings are waiting to be applied. The form shows the saved settings, which are not in effect yet.
ssh.enableHint: Each person also needs SSH access on their own account, which is set under Users.
ssh.offNote: The settings below are used when SSH is on.
ssh.portHint: The number SSH programs connect to. The usual one is 22; if you change it, tell your SSH program the new number.
ssh.portRequired: Enter a port number. The usual one is 22.
ssh.portRange: Enter a whole number from 1 to 65535.
ssh.portInUse: Port {{port}} is already used by this web interface. Choose another, such as 22.
ssh.password: Allow signing in with a password
ssh.key: Allow signing in with a key
ssh.keyHint: A key is a file on your computer that proves who you are, with no password to guess. Keys are added to each account under Users.
ssh.root: Allow the root account to sign in
ssh.rootHint: root is the built-in account with full control of the NAS. It is safer to leave this off and sign in with your own account.
ssh.forwardingHint: Lets someone signed in pass other network traffic through the NAS. Leave it off unless you use it.
ssh.compressionHint: Can speed up slow connections, at the cost of some processor time.
ssh.extraHint: These lines are added as they are to the SSH server's configuration file. A mistake can stop SSH from starting, so leave this empty unless you know you need it.
ssh.warnNoMethod: With both ways of signing in turned off, nobody can sign in over SSH. To stop SSH, turn it off at the top instead.
ssh.warnTurningOff: After you apply this, new SSH connections are refused. Anything that connects over SSH, such as a backup from another computer, stops working.
ssh.warnRootPassword: The root account can sign in with only a password. Anyone who guesses it controls the NAS. Turn off root sign-in, or allow keys only.
ssh.warnKeysOnly: Only people with a key on their account can sign in now. Check that yours is added before you apply.
ssh.saved: Saved. The changes take effect when you apply them in the band at the top of the page.
ssh.saveFailed: The SSH settings were not saved.
ssh.loadFailed: Could not read the SSH settings.

sharedFolders.title: Shared folders
sharedFolders.intro: Folders on your disks that other computers can reach over the network. To add, change or delete one, use the classic interface for now.
sharedFolders.addClassic: Add a shared folder in the classic interface
sharedFolders.usedNote: In use: a network share, backup job or other setting refers to this folder. Which one is not reported.

reason.ENOENT: Folder not found. Its disk may be disconnected or not mounted.
reason.ENOTDIR: The path leads to a file, not a folder.
reason.ENOENT_DB_MNTENT: Its file system is no longer set up on this NAS.

sharedFolders.loadFailed: Could not read the shared folders.
sharedFolders.empty: There are no shared folders yet. A shared folder is a folder on one of your disks that other computers can reach over the network.

account.passwordIntro: The new password works straight away; there is nothing to apply. It is the same account everywhere, so it also becomes your password for the classic interface and, if you use them, for shared folders on other computers.

reason.BAD_SECTOR: A few damaged areas (bad sectors). Keep your backup up to date and check this disk again soon.
reason.BAD_ATTRIBUTE_IN_THE_PAST: It was once used outside its safe limits, for example too hot. It reports no problem now.
reason.BAD_SECTOR_MANY: Many damaged areas (bad sectors). It may fail soon. Copy your data off it and replace it.

disks.title: Disks
disks.intro: The disks connected to the NAS and what each one holds. Open a disk to see its health, change its power settings or wipe it.

disks.useFailed: Could not check what the disks hold. No disk can be wiped until this has been checked.

disks.rescanFailed: Could not look for new disks.

use.fsCreating: A file system is being created
use.fsUnused: File system {{name}}, not used on this NAS

health.intro: Disk health is read only when you ask. Reading it wakes any disk that has gone to sleep to save power.

disk.title: Disk <device></device>
disk.subtitle: {{model}}, {{size}}
disk.notFound: No disk called {{name}} is connected. Its name may have changed when the NAS restarted.

fact.useShared: Shared folders or services use it.
fact.healthCheckLink: Check disk health on the Disk health page
fact.tempAtLimit: At or above its limit of {{limit}}
fact.tempAtAlert: At or above its alert level of {{alert}}
fact.removable: Removable while running (USB or a hot-swap bay)

names.intro: The device name ({{device}}) can change when the NAS restarts. These names stay the same.

disk.hardwareRaid: This is a set of disks made by a hardware RAID controller, which the NAS sees as one disk.

details.title: Health details
details.intro: Detailed readings come from the disk itself and are read only when you ask. Reading them wakes this disk if it has gone to sleep.
details.readAt: Read at {{time}}. The readings do not update by themselves.
details.noPassThrough: Some USB enclosures and virtual disks do not pass health readings through.
details.allWithin_one: The {{count}} reading is within the disk's limits.
details.allWithin_other: All {{count}} readings are within the disk's limits.

assess.pastBad: Was outside its limit in the past

5.name: Damaged areas replaced
5.meaning: Areas that went bad and were replaced by spare ones. A rising number is a warning sign.

197.name: Areas waiting to be checked
197.meaning: Areas the disk had trouble reading. It should be 0.

198.name: Areas that could not be read

199.name: Connection errors
199.meaning: Usually a loose or faulty cable, not the disk itself.

details.tableIntro: Value, Worst and Limit are the disk's own scores, usually counting down from 100 or 200. A reading is a problem when its value falls to its limit. The raw value is the disk's own count, which means something only for some readings.
details.noTable: This disk does not report a table of readings. NVMe and SAS disks report their health in another form, which is in the full report below.

result.interrupted: Interrupted, for example by a restart

details.testsEmpty: No self-test results are recorded on this disk.
details.testsEmptyHint: Some disks, such as NVMe disks, keep their results in a form shown only in the full report.
details.reportFailed: Could not read the full report.

monitoring.title: Monitoring
monitoring.watchHint: The NAS checks this disk regularly, records problems, and emails you about them when email is set up.
monitoring.globalOff: Monitoring is off for the whole NAS, so no disk is watched, even when this is ticked.
monitoring.hasTests_one: This disk has {{count}} scheduled self-test. Delete it under Scheduled self-tests below before you stop watching it.
monitoring.hasTests_other: This disk has {{count}} scheduled self-tests. Delete them under Scheduled self-tests below before you stop watching it.
monitoring.notInCheck: This disk did not report its health in the last check, so it may not support monitoring. Saving checks this.
monitoring.tempHint: Recorded at this temperature, and emailed at {{alert}}.
monitoring.tempRange: Enter a whole number from 1 to 100.
monitoring.loadFailed: Could not read whether this disk is watched.
monitoring.saveFailed: The monitoring setting was not saved.

tests.title: Scheduled self-tests
tests.empty: No self-tests are scheduled for this disk. A regular short test lets the disk find problems early.
tests.notWatched: Self-tests run only while the disk is watched.

power.title: Power settings
power.intro: These settings are for hard disks. Solid-state and NVMe disks usually ignore them.
power.notSet: The NAS does not set this disk's power settings now, so the disk uses its own.
power.noRemove: Once saved, these settings can be changed but not removed. The NAS then sends all four to the disk each time it starts or wakes.
power.spindownHint: When the disk has not been used for this long, it stops spinning to save power, and starts again when it is needed, which takes a few seconds. Some disks ignore this and keep spinning; the spin-down add-on (openmediavault-spindown) can put them to sleep after the same time.

apm.label: Power-saving level
apm.0: Off: the disk does not save power by itself

power.apmHint: How hard the disk itself works to save power. From level 128 up it does not spin down by itself. Many disks do not support this setting.
power.aamHint: Lets the disk move more quietly but more slowly. Many newer disks do not support this and ignore it.
power.writeCacheHint: Makes writing faster. If the power fails suddenly, the last few seconds of writes can be lost; a battery backup (UPS) protects against that. Most disks come with it on.
power.monitorWakes: Disk monitoring checks this disk every {{interval}} and wakes it to do so, so it may never stay asleep. To let it sleep, change what happens to sleeping disks in the disk health settings.
power.applyWakes: Applying sends these settings to the disk, which wakes it if it is asleep.
power.saveFailed: The power settings were not saved.

wipe.title: Wipe this disk
wipe.intro: Wiping erases everything on the disk so it can be used for something new, such as a new file system.

blocked.system: This is the system disk: openmediavault runs from it, so it cannot be wiped.
blocked.readOnly: This disk is read-only, so it cannot be wiped.
blocked.fsInUse: It holds the file system {{name}}, which is in use.
blocked.fsInUseDo: Stop using it and unmount it under File systems first.
blocked.fsSetUp: It holds the file system {{name}}, which is set up on this NAS.
blocked.fsSetUpDo: Remove it under File systems first.
blocked.fsCreating: A file system is being created on it now.
blocked.swap: It holds swap space, disk space the NAS can use as extra memory.
blocked.raid: It is part of the RAID array <array></array>. Wiping it would damage the array.
blocked.raidDo: Take it out of the array, or delete the array, on the array's page first.
blocked.unchecked: Could not check what this disk holds, so it cannot be wiped now.

wipe.fsLink: File systems in the classic interface
wipe.checking: Checking what is on this disk…
wipe.refusedTitle: This disk cannot be wiped now
wipe.changedBody: The disk now called {{device}} is not the one this page showed. Its details have been read again; check them before you wipe it.
wipe.goneBody: This disk is no longer connected.
wipe.consequence: Everything on this disk is erased: its partitions, file systems and files. This cannot be undone.

holds.fsUnused: The file system {{name}} ({{type}}, {{size}}). It is not used on this NAS. Its files are lost.
holds.none: No file system was found. Anything else on it, such as data from another computer, is erased too.
holds.untraceable: This NAS also has storage that this page cannot trace to a disk, such as encrypted disks, LVM or ZFS. If this disk is part of it, wiping it destroys that storage and its files.
holds.settingsKept: Its monitoring and power settings are kept.
holds.fsUnusedNoSize: The file system {{name}} ({{type}}). It is not used on this NAS. Its files are lost.

wipe.quickHint: Erases the partition table and the start and end of the disk, so the NAS sees it as empty. Takes a few seconds. The old files stay on the disk until they are overwritten, and recovery tools could still find them.
wipe.secureHint: Overwrites the whole disk once, so the old files cannot be recovered. Takes many hours: often 2 hours or more for each TB on a hard disk. You can stop it, but the disk is then only partly wiped. On a solid-state disk it may not reach every part of the disk.
wipe.secureReload: A secure wipe keeps running on the NAS if you reload this page or sign out, but this page can then no longer show it or stop it.
wipe.typeHint: The Wipe disk button is available once the name matches.
wipe.quickRunning: Quick wipe. This takes a few seconds.
wipe.secureRunning: Secure wipe. This takes many hours. You can leave this page or sign out; the wipe continues on the NAS. Its progress is shown here and in Tasks while you stay signed in.
wipe.stopBody: The part already overwritten stays erased; the rest of the disk is not wiped. Run a quick wipe afterwards so the NAS sees the disk as empty.
wipe.doneBody: It is now empty and ready to use. To store files on it, create a file system on it.
wipe.failedTitle: The wipe of {{device}} did not finish.
wipe.failedBody: Part of the disk may already be erased. Read the output for the reason.
wipe.stoppedBody: The part already overwritten is erased; the rest is not. Run a quick wipe so the NAS sees the disk as empty.

smart.title: Disk health
smart.intro: Whether the NAS watches your disks for signs of failure, and how it tells you.

overview.off: Monitoring is off. The NAS does not check your disks and will not tell you when one starts to fail.
overview.some: Monitoring is on for {{watched}} of {{total}} disks.
overview.all: Monitoring is on for every disk.
overview.emailOff: Email is not set up, so problems are only recorded in the NAS's log.
overview.emailLink: Email settings in the classic interface
overview.eventsNote: Alerts are sent only while "S.M.A.R.T." is ticked under Notification > Events in the classic interface (it is from the factory).
overview.eventsLink: Notification events in the classic interface
overview.emailFailed: Could not read the email settings.
overview.watchFailed_one: Could not read whether {{count}} disk is watched.
overview.watchFailed_other: Could not read whether {{count}} disks are watched.
overview.settingsFailed: Could not read the monitoring settings.
overview.classicLink: Disk health in the classic interface

settings.watchHint: The NAS checks each watched disk regularly, records problems in its log, and emails you when email is set up. Choose the disks to watch on the Overview or on each disk's page.
settings.watchOffWarn: With this off, no disk is checked and no self-test runs.
settings.intervalHint: How often the NAS checks each watched disk. Every 30 minutes suits most homes.
settings.intervalOdd: Now every {{seconds}} seconds, set elsewhere. Saving rounds it to whole minutes.
settings.intervalRange: Enter a whole number of minutes from 1 to 1440.
settings.asleep: When a disk is asleep at check time
settings.asleepHint: A disk that is asleep at every check is not checked until it is awake at one.
settings.asleepTestsRun: Scheduled self-tests still run, and wake the disk.
settings.asleepTestsSkipped: A self-test due while the disk is asleep is skipped too.

mode.never: Check it anyway; the check wakes the disk up
mode.sleep: Skip only disks in deep sleep; a disk that has only spun down is woken up
mode.standby: Skip the check, so the disk stays asleep (recommended)
mode.idle: Skip also while the disk is spinning but resting; checks happen only while it is busy

modeShort.never: Sleeping disks are woken for each check.
modeShort.sleep: Only disks in deep sleep are left asleep.
modeShort.idle: Resting and sleeping disks are left alone.

settings.tempWarn: Warn when a disk gets too hot
settings.tempHint: The NAS records it at this temperature and emails you at {{alert}}. Solid-state and NVMe disks often run hotter than hard disks; set their own limit on each disk's page.
settings.tempRange: Enter a whole number from 1 to 100.

tests.intro: A self-test is a check the disk runs on itself. A short test takes a few minutes; a long test reads the whole disk and takes hours. The disk keeps working meanwhile, a little slower. The NAS starts each test at its time; its result is in the disk's health details.

typeHint.S: A quick check of the disk's main parts. Takes a few minutes.
typeHint.L: Reads the whole disk. Takes hours on a large disk, and the disk is slower meanwhile.
typeHint.C: Looks for damage from shipping. Only some disks support it. Takes a few minutes.
typeHint.O: Updates the disk's own health readings. Takes a few minutes.

tests.runBodyLong: The disk reads its whole surface. This takes hours on a large disk, and the disk is slower meanwhile. It wakes up if it is asleep. Your files are not changed.
tests.runFailed: The test could not be started on {{device}}.

tests.loadFailed: Could not read the scheduled self-tests.
tests.empty: No self-tests are scheduled. A regular short test lets each disk find problems early.

fsGrow.intro: Use this after the storage under the file system has been made bigger, for example after adding a disk to its RAID array. The file system then uses all the space now available. If nothing was made bigger, nothing changes.

blocked.notMounted: It must be mounted to grow.
blocked.readOnly: It is read-only, so it cannot be grown.

fsGrow.consequence: It is made to use all the space on <device></device>. This cannot be undone: a file system cannot be made smaller again here.

blocked.sharedDo: Delete those shared folders, or move them to another file system, first.

multi.singleHintNoSize: Uses all the space, filling one disk after another. If any one disk fails, files on it are lost, and the file system may not open.

alerts.offLink: Notification settings in the classic interface

raidState.rebuildingNoDisk: A disk is missing. Rebuilding: {{progress}}. Until this ends it cannot lose another disk.

raidCreate.title: Create a RAID array
raidCreate.preflightBody: Apply or undo them before you create an array, so that only these changes are applied at the end.
raidCreate.looking: Looking for disks that can go into an array…
raidCreate.checkFailed: Could not check which disks can be used.
raidCreate.mixedSizes: These disks differ in size. Each counts as the smallest, {{size}}; {{lost}} on the larger ones is not used.
raidCreate.notEnough: An array needs at least two disks that can be erased. Connect more disks, or free some that are in use.
raidCreate.holdsUnknown: No file system was found, but the disk is not empty: it may hold old partitions, or be part of a RAID array from another computer.
raidCreate.cannotUsb: It is connected by USB. The RAID plugin does not use USB disks, because a USB connection can drop and break the array.
raidCreate.mirrorHint: Every file is kept on every disk. It can lose all but one disk. You can use the space of one disk: about {{usable}}.
raidCreate.raid5Hint: It can lose 1 disk. You can use all but one disk's space: about {{usable}}. If a second disk fails while it rebuilds, everything is lost.
raidCreate.raid6Hint: It can lose 2 disks. You can use all but two disks' space: about {{usable}}.
raidCreate.raid10Hint: Faster than parity. It can lose 1 disk, and sometimes more. You can use half the space: about {{usable}}.
raidCreate.mirrorHintNoSize: Every file is kept on every disk. It can lose all but one disk. You can use the space of one disk.
raidCreate.raid5HintNoSize: It can lose 1 disk. You can use all but one disk's space. If a second disk fails while it rebuilds, everything is lost.
raidCreate.raid6HintNoSize: It can lose 2 disks. You can use all but two disks' space.
raidCreate.raid10HintNoSize: Faster than parity. It can lose 1 disk, and sometimes more. You can use half the space.
raidCreate.stripeHint: No protection. If one disk fails, everything on all of them is lost. It uses all the space and is fast: about {{usable}}. It cannot be made bigger or repaired later.
raidCreate.stripeHintNoSize: No protection. If one disk fails, everything on all of them is lost. It uses all the space and is fast. It cannot be made bigger or repaired later.
raidCreate.combineAlt: For one large space without protection, Combine disks (BTRFS) under File systems can also join disks, so that a failed disk loses only the files on it.
raidCreate.useForFilesBody: Put a file system on it and mount it, so you can make shared folders on it.
raidCreate.useForFilesHint: Untick this to leave the array empty, for example to use it for something set up in the classic interface. You can add storage on it later.

sum.erase_one: Erase {{count}} disk. Everything on it is lost, including anything left on it from an earlier array:
sum.erase_other: Erase {{count}} disks. Everything on them is lost, including anything left on them from an earlier array:
sum.combine: Combine them into a new array: {{level}}. About {{usable}} can be used. {{protection}}
sum.sync: The disks then synchronise, which takes hours for large disks. The array can be used meanwhile, but it is not fully protected until this ends.
sum.stripeBody: If one disk fails, everything on all {{count}} disks is lost: every file on the array, not only the files on that disk. Keep a backup of anything you store on it.

create.ext4: Create an EXT4 file system on the array.
create.xfs: Create an XFS file system on the array.
create.btrfs: Create a BTRFS file system on the array.

sum.saveAndMount: Then save the array and mount the file system, which applies the changes for them. Nothing else is pending.
sum.save: Then save the array's settings, which applies the changes for it. Nothing else is pending.

raidCreate.typeHint: The button is available once the names match.

step.fsCandidate: Check the array can hold a file system
step.saveAndMount: Save the array and mount the new file system

fail.checkRead: Could not check the disks again, so nothing was erased.
fail.notCandidate: {{device}} was erased, but the RAID plugin still does not offer it for an array.
fail.createParts: The disks may now carry parts of an unfinished array. Creating again overwrites them.
fail.notFound: The array was created but has not appeared yet.
fail.listedLater: It is listed under RAID when it appears.
fail.fsCandidate: The new array is not offered for a file system yet.
fail.arrayStays: The array stays. You can add storage on it under File systems, or delete it on its page.
fail.saveAndMount: Saving the array and mounting the file system failed.
fail.saveBody: The changes are still saved and waiting in the band. The array already exists on the disks.
fail.notVerified: The NAS did not report the array, or its file system, as expected.
fail.fsCreate: Creating the file system on the array failed.
fail.clear: The new array could not be cleared.
fail.clearBody: Nothing else was erased. The array stays: you can add storage on it under File systems, or delete it on its page.

raidCreate.alsoBody: Also pending from elsewhere: {{list}}. Saving applies them too.
raidCreate.doneBody: RAID {{device}} ({{level}}, about {{size}}) is synchronising its disks. Its files can be used now; it is fully protected when this ends.
raidCreate.doneBodyStripe: RAID {{device}} (Stripe (RAID0), about {{size}}) is ready. It has no protection: if one disk fails, everything on it is lost.
raidCreate.doneFs: {{name}} is mounted and ready, with {{size}} free.
raidCreate.chooseLevel: Choose how to protect your files.

sec.replace: Adding a disk replaces the missing one. The NAS then rebuilds onto it.
sec.spare: Adding a disk keeps it as a spare: it waits, and the NAS rebuilds onto it by itself when a disk fails. It does not add space.
sec.either: Adding a disk can keep it as a spare, or make the array bigger.

blocked.level: A {{level}} array cannot take more disks here.
blocked.notRunning: It is not running, so no disk can be added.
blocked.rebuilding: It is rebuilding onto {{disk}} now. Wait until this ends.
blocked.rebuildingNoDisk: It is rebuilding now. Wait until this ends.
blocked.busy: It is busy now ({{what}}). Wait until this ends.

raidAdd.title: Add a disk to RAID {{device}}
raidAdd.looking: Looking for disks that can be added…

fixed.replace: The disk replaces the missing one.
fixed.spare: The disk is kept as a spare.

raidAdd.purposeChoose: Choose what the disk is for.
raidAdd.purposeSpareHint: It waits, and the NAS rebuilds onto it by itself when a disk fails. It adds no space. You can take it out again later.
raidAdd.purposeBiggerHint: Adds about {{added}} for each disk. Reshaping the array takes many hours, often a day or more for large disks, and cannot be undone. The file system on it is grown afterwards, on its page.
raidAdd.cannotSmall: It is smaller than the array's disks ({{size}}). A disk added to an array must be at least as large as the smallest one.
raidAdd.none: No disk can be added right now. Connect a disk at least {{size}} large, or free one that is in use.
raidAdd.removedNote: A disk taken out of an array keeps the array's marks, so it is offered under Erase and reuse: it is erased first.

sum.replace: Add it to RAID {{array}} in place of the missing disk. The NAS then copies {{size}} onto it to rebuild the array. This takes hours on a large disk; the array can be used meanwhile, and it is protected again when this ends.
sum.spare: Add it to RAID {{array}} as a spare. It waits, and the NAS rebuilds onto it by itself when a disk fails.
sum.bigger: Add them to RAID {{array}} and reshape it to use them: it becomes about {{new}} (now {{size}}). Reshaping cannot be undone and takes many hours, often a day or more. Do not turn off the NAS until it ends. The array can be used meanwhile, and its size grows only when the reshape ends.
sum.growFs: Then grow the file system on it, on the file system's page, so it uses the new space.
sum.takeOutFailed: Then take the failed disk {{device}} ({{model}}, serial number {{serial}}) out of the array, so you can disconnect it.
sum.save: Then save the array's settings, which applies the changes for it. Nothing else is pending.

step.check: Check the disk and the array again
step.grow: Add the disks and reshape the array
step.takeOut: Take the failed disk out of the array

fail.arrayChanged: RAID {{array}} changed since you chose the disk. Nothing was erased.
fail.addBody: The disk then shows as empty.
fail.spareOnly: {{device}} was added as a spare, but the array was not made bigger.
fail.spareStays: The disk stays as a spare. To use it otherwise, take it out on the array's page.
fail.notReported: The NAS did not report the disk in the array as expected.
fail.takeOut: The new disk was added, but taking out the failed disk failed.
fail.takeOutLater: The failed disk can be taken out later on the array's page.

done.replaceBody: The NAS is copying everything onto {{device}}. Follow it on the array's page; it takes hours on a large disk. You can leave this page or sign out.
done.disconnect: You can now disconnect {{device}} ({{model}}, serial number {{serial}}).
done.spareTitle: {{device}} is now a spare of RAID {{array}}.
done.spareBody: It takes over by itself when a disk fails.
done.biggerBody: RAID {{array}} becomes about {{new}} when it ends, which can take a day or more. Do not turn off the NAS until then. Afterwards, grow the file system on it so it uses the new space.

blocked.rebuilding: It is being rebuilt now. Wait until this ends.
blocked.level: A {{level}} array keeps no spare copy, so taking out a disk would destroy it.
blocked.degraded: The array is already missing a disk. Taking out another would leave it without protection, or destroy it.
blocked.busy: It is busy now ({{what}}). Wait until this ends.
blocked.notRunning: It is not running, so no disk can be taken out.
blocked.role: What this disk is doing is not known, so it cannot be taken out.

raidRemove.refusedTitle: This disk cannot be taken out now
raidRemove.gone: This disk is no longer in the array.
raidRemove.failedBody: It has failed and holds no part of the working array, so nothing is lost. Afterwards you can disconnect it.
raidRemove.spareBody: The array then has no spare. Nothing is lost.
raidRemove.notErased: The disk is not erased: it keeps the array's marks. Wipe it before you use it for something else.
raidRemove.workingTitle: Take working disk {{device}} out of RAID {{array}}?
raidRemove.consequence: The array then runs without that disk and loses protection. {{protection}}
raidRemove.ifAnother: No file is lost now. If another disk fails before a new one is added and rebuilt, {{loss}}

loss.all: everything on the array is lost.
loss.oneMore: it can still lose one more.

raidRemove.spareFirst: To replace a disk that still works, add the new disk as a spare first; then take this one out, and the NAS rebuilds onto the spare at once.
raidRemove.notErasedShort: The disk is not erased: it keeps the array's marks.
raidRemove.typeHint: The button is available once the name matches.
raidRemove.doneBody: You can now disconnect it (serial number {{serial}}). It still carries the array's marks: wipe it before you use it for something else, and before it can go into an array again.
raidRemove.doneApply: Apply the pending changes so the NAS remembers the array without it when it next starts.
raidRemove.undo: To undo this, add the disk again: it is offered under Erase and reuse, is erased first, and the array then rebuilds onto it.
raidRemove.unknown: Could not tell whether the disk was taken out.

raidCheck.title: Check this array
raidCheck.intro: A check reads every disk of the array and compares the copies, to find damage before a disk is needed for a rebuild. It changes nothing. Run it every month or so. It takes about as long as reading one whole disk, often many hours, and the NAS is slower meanwhile. It wakes the disks.

blocked.busy: It is busy now ({{what}}). Wait until this ends.
blocked.degraded: A degraded array cannot be checked. Replace its missing disk first.
blocked.notRunning: It is not running, so it cannot be checked.

raidCheck.ended: The check ended at {{time}}. Any differences it found are written to the system log.
raidCheck.dialogBody: The NAS reads every disk of the array and compares the copies. Nothing is changed. It takes many hours for large disks, and the NAS is slower meanwhile. The disks are woken and kept busy until it ends. You can leave this page or sign out; the check goes on on the NAS.
raidCheck.stopBody: The check stops where it is. Nothing is changed. You can start it again later, from the beginning.
raidCheck.notIdle: The array is no longer idle, so the check was not started.
raidCheck.notChecking: The array is no longer being checked.

raidDelete.title: Delete this array
raidDelete.intro: Deleting breaks up the array. Its disks are freed for other use, and everything stored on the array is lost.

blocked.fs: It holds the file system {{name}}, which is set up on this NAS.
blocked.fsDo: Unmount it, or remove it from the NAS, on its page first.
blocked.creating: A file system is being created on it now.
blocked.other: Other storage is built on it, such as LVM.
blocked.unread: Could not check what this array holds, so it cannot be deleted now.

raidDelete.checking: Checking what is on this array…
raidDelete.refusedTitle: This array cannot be deleted now
raidDelete.consequence: Everything stored on this array is lost, and the array cannot be put back together. This cannot be undone.

onIt.fs: The file system {{name}} ({{type}}). It is not used on this NAS. Its files are lost.
onIt.nothing: No file system was found on it. Anything else on it is lost too.
onIt.disks: Its disks are not wiped: the files on them cannot be read without the array, but are not overwritten either. Wipe a disk before you give it away.

raidDelete.typeHint: The button is available once the name matches.
raidDelete.doneBody: Its disks are free: {{list}}. Apply the pending changes so the NAS forgets the array when it next starts.
raidDelete.maybeStopped: If the array was stopped but not deleted, it shows as not running after a refresh.
raidDelete.unknown: Could not tell whether the array was deleted.
